title: Magma ocean cools and the first crust forms
description: The energy of the Moon-forming impact is thought to have left Earth covered by an ocean of molten rock, which then cooled to form a solid crust. Zircon crystals with ages near 4.4 billion years show that crust existed by then, so any global melting must have come earlier.
uncertainty: The magma ocean has not been dated directly; its timing is inferred from the age of the Moon-forming impact and of the oldest zircons.

title: Oldest known mineral grains and signs of early oceans
description: A zircon crystal from the Jack Hills of Western Australia has a uranium-lead age of 4,404 million years, the oldest known material formed on Earth. Its oxygen isotopes suggest the magma it grew in had interacted with liquid water, pointing to continental-type crust and oceans very early on.
uncertainty: The age is 4,404 plus or minus 8 million years for a single grain; that oceans existed is an inference from its chemistry, and the grains survive inside much younger sedimentary rock.

title: Nuvvuagittuq rocks, possibly the oldest on Earth
description: Volcanic rocks of the Nuvvuagittuq Greenstone Belt on Hudson Bay may be the only surviving pieces of crust from the Hadean eon. A 2025 study dated an intrusion that cuts through them to about 4,157 million years.
uncertainty: The age is disputed: published estimates range from about 3,750 to 4,388 million years, depending on the dating method and how it is interpreted.

title: Oldest undisputed rocks: the Acasta Gneiss
description: The Acasta Gneisses of northwestern Canada are the oldest rocks whose age is generally accepted, dated radiometrically to 4.03 billion years.
uncertainty: The 4.03 billion year figure is firm for the oldest parts of the complex; older ages claimed for other rocks, such as Nuvvuagittuq, are disputed.

title: First stable continental cores (cratons)
description: Thick, stable blocks of continental crust called cratons were assembled during the Archean and still form the cores of today's continents. The Kaapvaal Craton of southern Africa, one of the best preserved, was built in stages between about 3.5 and 2.5 billion years ago.
uncertainty: Cratons formed at different times in different places; the span given is for the Kaapvaal Craton, and older fragments of crust exist elsewhere.

title: Earliest firm evidence of Earth's magnetic field
description: Tiny magnetic inclusions in 3.4 to 3.45 billion-year-old volcanic rocks from South Africa record a magnetic field, showing that the dynamo in Earth's liquid core was already running. The field shields the atmosphere from the solar wind.
uncertainty: Magnetism in Jack Hills zircons has been read as evidence of a field 4.2 billion years ago, but other researchers find those grains were remagnetised later, so the field's existence before about 3.5 billion years ago is contested.

title: Plate tectonics takes hold (debated)
description: Earth's outer shell broke into rigid plates that move, collide and sink back into the mantle. A review of sedimentary, igneous, metamorphic and magnetic evidence finds the major shift in Earth's behaviour in the middle to late Archean.
uncertainty: The start of plate tectonics is one of the most debated dates in geology, with estimates ranging from the Hadean (before 4 billion years ago) to the Neoproterozoic (less than 1 billion years ago).

title: Great Oxidation Event
description: Free oxygen built up in the atmosphere for the first time, a change recorded in the chemistry of sedimentary rocks. Precise dating of volcanic rocks in South Africa places the onset between about 2,460 and 2,426 million years ago, with oxygen levels oscillating for some 200 million years afterwards.
uncertainty: The onset was moved about 100 million years earlier by this dating; the rise was not a single step, and the end is usually tied to the close of a carbon-isotope excursion about 2.06 billion years ago.

title: Huronian glaciation
description: At least three ice ages are recorded by glacial deposits in the Huronian rocks north of Lake Huron in Canada, laid down between about 2.4 and 2.1 billion years ago. They are among the oldest known glaciations and overlap with the first rise of atmospheric oxygen.
uncertainty: The individual ice ages are poorly dated, and how many of them were global is uncertain.

title: Supercontinent Columbia (Nuna) assembles
description: Most of the existing continental blocks are thought to have joined into one landmass, called Columbia or Nuna, through worldwide mountain-building collisions. The reconstruction rests on matching belts of rock of this age and on magnetic data from different continents.
uncertainty: Columbia is a hypothetical reconstruction first proposed in 2002; its exact layout and how long it lasted (to perhaps 1.5 billion years ago) are uncertain.

title: Vredefort impact
description: An asteroid struck what is now South Africa, creating the largest confirmed impact structure on Earth, originally perhaps 170 to 300 km across. The eroded central uplift, the Vredefort Dome, has been dated to 2,023 million years.
uncertainty: The age carries an uncertainty of about 4 million years; the original crater size is an estimate because the structure is deeply eroded.
place: Vredefort Dome, Free State, South Africa

title: Sudbury impact
description: A body roughly 10 to 15 km across hit what is now Ontario, Canada, leaving one of the largest and oldest known impact structures, about 130 km in diameter. The melted rock it produced hosts major nickel and copper ores and has been dated radiometrically.

title: Supercontinent Rodinia assembles
description: The continents came together again as the supercontinent Rodinia, which later broke up between about 750 and 633 million years ago. Its existence is inferred from mountain belts of matching age and from magnetic data.
uncertainty: Rodinia's existence is widely accepted but reconstructions of how the continents were arranged within it still differ in many details.

title: Neoproterozoic rise in oxygen
description: Oxygen in the atmosphere and oceans rose a second time, toward modern levels, as recorded by changes in the chemistry of marine sediments.
uncertainty: The start and end are only roughly known, and the causes are still debated.

title: Sturtian glaciation (Snowball Earth)
description: Ice sheets reached sea level in the tropics and the planet stayed largely frozen for about 58 million years, the longer of the two Cryogenian 'Snowball Earth' glaciations. Glacial deposits of this age occur on many continents and are dated by uranium-lead and rhenium-osmium methods.
uncertainty: The start and end dates are well constrained; how complete the ice cover was (fully frozen oceans or a belt of open water near the equator) is still debated.

title: Pannotia, a possible short-lived supercontinent
description: Some reconstructions join the continents into a brief supercontinent called Pannotia near the end of the Precambrian, breaking apart about 560 million years ago as the Iapetus Ocean opened.
uncertainty: Pannotia's existence is disputed: a 2022 study argues it never fully formed because it began to break up before it was assembled.

title: Marinoan glaciation (Snowball Earth)
description: A second global glaciation covered the continents with ice down to the tropics. It ended about 635 million years ago with rapid melting, marked by a distinctive layer of carbonate rock whose base defines the start of the Ediacaran Period.
uncertainty: The end is tightly dated (636.0 to 634.7 million years ago) but the onset is only known to lie between 649.9 and 639.0 million years ago.

title: Gondwana assembles
description: Collisions between older continental blocks built the southern supercontinent Gondwana, which included today's South America, Africa, Arabia, India, Antarctica and Australia. The mountain belts formed in these collisions are dated across those continents.
uncertainty: Assembly was gradual, starting with earlier collisions about 800 to 650 million years ago; the dates given are for the final stage.

title: Pangaea assembles
description: Gondwana, Euramerica and Siberia merged into the supercontinent Pangaea, which stretched nearly from pole to pole and was surrounded by a single ocean. The fit of the continents, matching rocks and fossils, and magnetic data all record it.
uncertainty: Assembly was gradual, so 335 million years ago is an approximate, commonly quoted figure.

title: Emeishan Traps eruptions
description: Flood basalts cover a large area of what is now Sichuan and Yunnan in China, with the main eruptions between 262 and 261 million years ago.
uncertainty: The start is given as 265 million years ago or earlier; the end, at 259 million years ago, is better fixed.

title: Siberian Traps eruptions
description: One of the largest volcanic outpourings known flooded Siberia with lava. Uranium-lead dating shows that about two-thirds of the lava erupted in roughly 300,000 years, before and during the end-Permian mass extinction, with eruptions continuing for at least 500,000 years after it.
uncertainty: The dating is precise to about a tenth of a million years; that the eruptions caused the extinction is strongly supported by the timing but the exact mechanism is still studied.

title: Central Atlantic Magmatic Province
description: As Pangaea began to split, magma intruded and erupted across a vast area on what are now four continents. Uranium-lead ages show the activity began about 100,000 years before the oldest known lava flows and coincided with the end-Triassic extinction, dated at 201.51 million years ago.
uncertainty: The extinction horizon is dated to within about 0.15 million years; the eruptions came in pulses over several hundred thousand years.

title: Pangaea breaks up and the Atlantic begins to open
description: Rifting between North America and northwest Africa split Pangaea, and new ocean floor began to form in the central Atlantic. The South and North Atlantic opened later, and the ocean is still widening today.
uncertainty: The timing of the first ocean floor is controversial, with estimates from 200 to 170 million years ago; rift basins had begun to open earlier, in the Late Triassic.

title: Selli Event: the oceans lose their oxygen
description: Much of the deep ocean runs out of oxygen at the start of the Aptian age, leaving black shales worldwide and killing off marine species; it is linked to large volcanic eruptions and warming.

title: Ontong Java Plateau forms
description: Eruptions on the floor of the Pacific build an oceanic plateau that, with the Manihiki and Hikurangi plateaus, covered about 1% of the Earth's surface, among the largest volcanic outpourings known.
uncertainty: Published ages for the main eruptions range from about 125 to 116 million years ago.

title: Western Interior Seaway divides North America
description: With sea level high, an inland sea runs from the Gulf of Mexico to the Arctic Ocean and splits North America into two landmasses, Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east.

title: Cenomanian–Turonian boundary event
description: The most recent truly global loss of oxygen from the oceans disturbs the carbon cycle and causes an extinction of marine life.
uncertainty: Estimates fall between about 94.5 and 93 million years ago; the stage boundary itself is dated to 93.9 million years ago.

title: Deccan Traps eruptions
description: Huge volumes of basalt lava erupted across what is now western India, building one of the largest volcanic provinces on Earth. Radiometric dating places the eruptions in a span of 600,000 to 800,000 years across the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary.
uncertainty: The dates are precise, but how much the eruptions contributed to the end-Cretaceous extinction, compared with the Chicxulub impact, is debated.

title: Chicxulub impact
description: An asteroid about 10 km across struck the Yucatan, leaving a buried crater roughly 180 to 200 km wide. Argon-argon dating puts the impact at 66.04 million years ago, matching the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary and its worldwide iridium-rich layer and mass extinction.
uncertainty: The age is 66.043 million years with an uncertainty of about 0.043 million years.

title: Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum
description: A massive release of carbon into the ocean and atmosphere caused rapid global warming and ocean acidification. It is recorded in deep-sea sediments worldwide as a sharp shift in carbon isotopes and dissolved carbonate.
uncertainty: The date is well established; the source of the carbon (volcanism, methane hydrates or both) is still debated.

title: India collides with Asia and the Himalaya begin to rise
description: After drifting north for tens of millions of years, the Indian plate ran into Eurasia. Neither continent could sink beneath the other, so the crust crumpled and thickened to build the Himalaya and the Tibetan Plateau.
uncertainty: The USGS gives a range of 40 to 50 million years ago; the date of first contact is debated and other studies give different figures.

title: Antarctica freezes over
description: A continental ice sheet grew rapidly on Antarctica at the Eocene-Oligocene boundary, with a marked global cooling recorded in deep-sea sediments. Climate modelling points to falling atmospheric carbon dioxide as the main cause.
uncertainty: The date of glaciation is firm; whether the opening of Southern Ocean gateways such as the Drake Passage also played a part is debated, and the date of that opening is poorly known.

title: Messinian salinity crisis
description: The Mediterranean was progressively cut off from the Atlantic and partly dried up, leaving very thick salt deposits. Astronomically tuned sediment layers date the onset to 5.96 million years ago and the return of normal marine conditions to 5.33 million years ago.
uncertainty: The onset is dated to within 0.02 million years; how far the sea level fell and how the basin refilled are still debated.

title: Isthmus of Panama closes
description: Rising land joined North and South America, cutting the sea link between the Atlantic and Pacific and letting land animals cross between the continents. A review of geological, fossil and genetic evidence dates the complete land bridge to about 2.8 million years ago.
uncertainty: The date is disputed: some geological studies argue that the seaway closed much earlier, in the middle Miocene, about 15 to 13 million years ago.

title: Quaternary ice ages begin
description: Large ice sheets began to grow and retreat repeatedly across the northern continents, a cycle that continues today. The start of the Quaternary Period is formally set at 2.58 million years ago, at a marker layer at Monte San Nicola in Sicily.
uncertainty: The 2.58 million year boundary is a formal definition; Northern Hemisphere glaciation intensified gradually around that time rather than in a single step.

title: Last Glacial Maximum
description: Ice sheets reached their greatest extent of the last glacial period, covering much of northern North America and northern Europe. Radiocarbon and exposure dating of glacial deposits worldwide fix the timing.
uncertainty: Ice sheets peaked at somewhat different times in different regions; a widely cited compilation gives 26,500 to about 19,000 years ago.

title: End of the last glacial period (start of the Holocene)
description: An abrupt warming ended the Younger Dryas cold spell and the last glacial period. The boundary is defined at a depth of 1,492.45 m in the NGRIP2 ice core from central Greenland, where an abrupt shift in hydrogen isotopes marks the end of the cold spell.
uncertainty: The age is a formal definition by the International Commission on Stratigraphy, ratified in 2008; the underlying ice-core dating has a small uncertainty.
